title: Charts with AI: the Chart Prompt Guide
subtitle: Pick the right chart for your question, prompt any AI tool to draw it, and check it before you share.
headline: Charts with AI.
Right chart, right prompt.
intro: The 12 charts you'll use most, each with a picture, when to use it, the common mistake and a ready prompt. About 1 hour 15 minutes.
description: Built from the IMS team's Chart Prompt Guide. Two short lessons teach the method, then 12 short lessons each show one chart on made-up sample data, when to use it, the mistake to avoid, and a ready prompt you can paste into ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot. A one-page finder covers all 33 charts in the guide.
The course text, pictures, sample data and tests were generated with AI and checked against the guide. All numbers belong to a fictional team, so you can practise freely.
outcomes: Pick the right chart from the question you need to answer
Write a 4-part prompt that AI tools follow: type, data, layout, style
Use the 12 charts a contact-center team needs most, from Ranked Bar to Pareto
Make any tool match the Kalam look with one style block
Check the data and the generated chart before you share it
requirements: Any AI chat tool (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) or Excel
No design or data background needed
audience: Team leaders and supervisors who report results
Anyone who presents numbers to a manager or client

sections.title: The method
sections.covers: Ask for the chart in 4 parts, then check it
sections.summary: Pick the chart from your question, write a 4-part prompt, and check the data and the result.

lessons.title: Ask for the chart in 4 parts
lessons.alt: Pareto chart of 180 abandoned calls by client on made-up Team Nova data, used as the worked example.

blocks.p: What do you need to show: a ranking, a trend, a result against target, the few causes behind a problem? The question picks the chart. The next modules cover the 12 charts you will use most.

1 · Chart type: "A Pareto chart ranking…". 2 · Real data: every label and number, or the tool invents them. 3 · Layout and labels: order, highlight, axis from zero, "to scale". 4 · Style: paste the style block below.

blocks.h: Example: the prompt behind the picture
blocks.code: A Pareto chart of 180 abandoned calls in January 2026 by client, descending bars Atlas 72, Birch 45, Cedar 27, Dune 18, Ember 9, Fjord 6, Gale 3; an amber cumulative line on a 0–100% right axis passing 40%, 65% and 80%; a dashed 80% reference line; the top three bars highlighted in plum, the rest in lilac; a callout 'Atlas + Birch + Cedar = 80% of abandoned', clean modern flat design. + style block

blocks.h: Style block: paste it after every prompt
blocks.code: Style: Kalam brand look. Warm off-white background #FBFAF8. Primary deep plum #4A154B with a plum gradient #7A3479 → #3A0F3B; secondary mauve #A36A9F; soft lilac fills #D9C2D8 and #F2DFF0. One accent only: amber #C26A1F (gradient #E5934A → #A9521A), used just for the key problem or insight. Text ink #1D1424, muted labels #6B6275, hairline borders #E8E2E8. Font DM Sans: bold titles, regular labels, small UPPERCASE letter-spaced section labels in plum. White rounded cards (12–14 px radius) with a soft shadow, lots of white space, thin light gridlines, values labeled directly on the chart, flat vector, no 3D, no clutter, 16:9 landscape. Use exactly the numbers given; do not add or change values.

lessons.title: Check it before you share it

blocks.h: Before you prompt: check the data
blocks.p: Parts add up to the total (1,900 + 700 + 400 = 3,000). Every rate has its count and base: "8.4% (64 of 760)". The period is in the title, and partial weeks or months are marked.

blocks.h: After the tool draws it: check the chart
blocks.p: Every number and label matches your data. Bars start at zero. The title says the finding ("Three clients make up 80% of abandoned calls"), not just the topic. One highlight colour only. Nothing overlaps.
Image tools often change numbers or put labels on the wrong bar. For exact charts, build them in Excel or Power BI and use AI for the prompt and the layout.

questions.q: What are the four parts of a good chart prompt, in order?
o: Chart type, real data, layout and labels, style
questions.e: Name the chart and its job, give every number, say how to lay it out and label it, then paste the style block.

questions.q: Your prompt says 'a bar chart of abandoned calls by client' but gives no numbers. What will most AI tools do?
questions.e: No number in the prompt means the tool invents one. Write every label and value exactly.

questions.q: Which title is best for a chart?
o: Three clients make up 80% of abandoned calls
questions.e: A good title says the finding, not just the topic, and the eyebrow line gives the scope and period.

questions.q: A rate is shown as '33%'. What should you add next to it?
o: Its count and base, for example 33% (1 of 3)
questions.e: 33% from 3 calls and 33% from 300 calls are not the same evidence. Show n with every rate.

questions.q: An image tool made your chart. What must you do before sharing it?
o: Nothing, the tool used your prompt
Check every text and number label against your data
questions.e: Generated images often get labels and numbers wrong. For exact data, build the chart in Excel or Power BI.

sections.title: Compare and explain
sections.covers: 6 charts: Ranked Bar, Bullet, Stacked Bar, Waterfall, Flowchart, Decision Matrix
sections.summary: Rank people and items, show results against target, split and explain totals, map a process and choose between options.
topics: You want to rank people or items from highest to lowest.
You show actual results against a target in a compact way.
You compare groups and also show how each total splits into parts.
You explain how a total moved from one value to another, step by step.
You need to show a decision process step by step, with yes/no branches.
You must pick between options measured on the same criteria.

lessons.title: Ranked Bar
lessons.alt: Ranked Bar example on made-up Team Nova data. A ranked horizontal bar chart of calls handled per interpreter, January 2026, sorted high to low, bars starting at zero.

blocks.p: You want to rank people or items from highest to lowest.
Bars start at zero; sort by value, never alphabetically.

blocks.code: A ranked horizontal bar chart of calls handled per interpreter, January 2026, sorted high to low, bars starting at zero: Int-07 212, Int-03 198, Int-11 176, Int-02 160, Int-09 151, Int-05 140, Int-12 122, Int-04 95; top three bars in plum, the rest in lilac, value labels at the bar ends, a callout 'Top 3 = 47%, 586 of 1,254 calls', clean modern flat design. + style block

lessons.title: Bullet Chart
lessons.alt: Bullet Chart example on made-up Team Nova data. A bullet chart of February 2026 actual vs target, one row per measure with grey background bands.

blocks.p: You show actual results against a target in a compact way.
Say clearly when lower is better (e.g. missed calls).

blocks.code: A bullet chart of February 2026 actual vs target, one row per measure with grey background bands: Service level 82.0% vs target 80% (higher is better, met, plum); Abandoned rate 7.1% vs 5% (lower is better, not met, amber); Late answers 6.2% vs 8% (lower is better, met); Missed 3.6% vs 4% (lower is better, met); a black target marker on each row, '✓ met' or '✗ not met' at the right, footnote 'sample targets', clean dashboard style. + style block

lessons.title: Stacked Bar
lessons.alt: Stacked Bar example on made-up Team Nova data. A 100% stacked horizontal bar chart of ring outcomes by shift, January 2026.

blocks.p: You compare groups and also show how each total splits into parts.
Rounded shares may not add to 100%; label every segment, even tiny ones.

blocks.code: A 100% stacked horizontal bar chart of ring outcomes by shift, January 2026: Day 1,800 rings: on time 92.2%, late 5.0%, missed 2.8%; Evening 680 rings: 83.8%, 10.3%, 5.9%; Night 340 rings: 74.7%, 16.5%, 8.8%; on time in plum, late in mauve, missed in amber; labels inside large segments and beside tiny ones, a note that rounded shares may not add to 100%, plum, lilac and amber palette. + style block

lessons.title: Waterfall
lessons.alt: Waterfall example on made-up Team Nova data. A waterfall chart of abandoned calls from January 180 to February 199.

blocks.p: You explain how a total moved from one value to another, step by step.
Non-zero axis is acceptable here only with a break mark and a note; check that rounded steps still reconcile.

blocks.code: A waterfall chart of abandoned calls from January 180 to February 199: start bar 180 in plum, then floating steps by client Atlas −12 (lilac), Birch +19 (amber), Cedar −9 (lilac), Dune +9 (amber), Others +12 (amber), end bar 199 in plum; dotted connector lines, value labels, y-axis starting at 150 with a break mark and the note 'axis starts at 150; −12 + 19 − 9 + 9 + 12 = +19', clean modern flat design. + style block

lessons.title: Flowchart
lessons.alt: Flowchart example on made-up Team Nova data. A flowchart of what happens to a call, January 2026.

blocks.p: You need to show a decision process step by step, with yes/no branches.
Every diamond needs exactly two labeled exits.

blocks.code: A flowchart of what happens to a call, January 2026: 'Call arrives 3,000' → diamond 'Caller waits?' (No → 'Abandoned 180') → 'Ring interpreter 2,820' → diamond 'Picked up?' (No → 'Missed 120' → grey box 'Re-route to next, no counts in the data') → diamond 'Within 5 s?' (Yes → 'On time 2,484', No → 'Late 216'); every diamond with two labeled exits Yes/No, problem boxes in amber, clean professional vector style. + style block

lessons.title: Decision Matrix
lessons.alt: Decision Matrix example on made-up Team Nova data. A decision matrix heat grid of projected occupancy from a scenario model.

blocks.p: You must pick between options measured on the same criteria.
These are projections, not scores; higher occupancy is not always better (it can slow answers).

blocks.code: A decision matrix heat grid of projected occupancy from a scenario model: rows 'Route as today', 'Bilinguals as overflow', 'Shared pool first'; columns 'Current roster', '+2 evening', '+2 night'; values 72/70/68, 76/74/71, 81/79/75 %; darker plum = higher; the 81% cell outlined in amber with the note 'above the 80% ceiling'; footnote 'model projection, not actuals or scores'; flat design. + style block

questions.q: How should a ranked bar chart of calls per interpreter be sorted?
o: By value, highest first, with bars starting at zero
questions.e: Sort by value, never alphabetically, and start bars at zero.

questions.q: In a bullet chart for abandoned rate, actual 7.1% and target 5%. What must the row say?
o: Lower is better, and the target is not met
questions.e: Say clearly when lower is better. 7.1% is above the 5% target, so it is not met.

questions.q: Abandoned calls went from 180 to 199. The waterfall steps are −12, +19, −9, +9 and +12. What should you check?
o: That the axis starts at zero
That the steps add up to the total change: +19

questions.q: In a flowchart, what must every decision diamond have?
o: Exactly two labeled exits, like Yes and No
questions.e: Every diamond needs exactly two labeled exits so the reader always knows where to go.

questions.q: In the decision matrix, the 'Shared pool first, current roster' cell shows 81%. What is it?
o: A projected occupancy from a model, not an actual result or a score
questions.e: Matrix cells here are model projections. Higher occupancy is not always better: it can slow answers.

sections.title: Trends, causes and patterns
sections.covers: 6 charts: Line / Area, Pareto, Heatmap, Histogram, Scatter Plot, Funnel
sections.summary: See the trend, find the few causes behind most of a problem, spot when it clusters, and check spread, links and drop-offs.
topics: You want the overall trend of one measure over time.
You want to find the few causes behind most of a problem.
You want to see when or where a problem clusters across two dimensions.
You want to see how values are spread, not just the average.
You check whether two measures move together, item by item.
Each stage is a real step and you want to see where volume drops.

lessons.title: Line / Area
lessons.alt: Line / Area example on made-up Team Nova data. A line and area chart of Team Nova offered calls per week, weeks starting Monday.

blocks.p: You want the overall trend of one measure over time.
Mark partial periods; don't read them as a trend.

blocks.code: A line and area chart of Team Nova offered calls per week, weeks starting Monday: 29 Dec 210 (partial week, hollow dot), 5 Jan 640, 12 Jan 702, 19 Jan 688, 26 Jan 731, 2 Feb 815 (peak, label in amber), 9 Feb 390 (partial week, hollow dot); plum line over a soft lilac area, y-axis 0 to 1,000, value labels on each point, light gridlines, legend 'full week / partial week', title 'Offered calls climbed to a peak of 815 in the week of 2 Feb', clean modern flat design. + style block

lessons.title: Pareto
lessons.alt: Pareto example on made-up Team Nova data. A Pareto chart of 180 abandoned calls in January 2026 by client, descending bars Atlas 72, Birch 45, Cedar 27, Dune 18, Ember 9, Fjord 6, Gale 3; an amber cumulative line on a 0–100% right axis passing 40%, 65% and 80%; a dashed 80% reference line; the top three bars highlighted in plum, the rest in lilac; a callout 'Atlas + Birch + Cedar = 80% of abandoned', clean modern flat design..

blocks.p: You want to find the few causes behind most of a problem.
Use counts of causes, not percentages or averages.

blocks.code: A Pareto chart of 180 abandoned calls in January 2026 by client, descending bars Atlas 72, Birch 45, Cedar 27, Dune 18, Ember 9, Fjord 6, Gale 3; an amber cumulative line on a 0–100% right axis passing 40%, 65% and 80%; a dashed 80% reference line; the top three bars highlighted in plum, the rest in lilac; a callout 'Atlas + Birch + Cedar = 80% of abandoned', clean modern flat design. + style block

lessons.title: Heatmap
lessons.alt: Heatmap example on made-up Team Nova data. An hourly heatmap mock-up of abandoned rate, days Mon–Sun as rows and two-hour blocks 00–22 as columns, single-hue lilac-to-plum scale 0–20% with values in each cell, higher at night (00–06) and on Friday and Saturday evenings; hatched grey cells for slots with fewer than 5 calls, a legend stating that cut-off, subtitle 'illustrative mock-up, values invented', clean data-visualization style..

blocks.p: You want to see when or where a problem clusters across two dimensions.
The '< 3 calls' cut-off is an example, not a standard; choose and state your own.

blocks.code: An hourly heatmap mock-up of abandoned rate, days Mon–Sun as rows and two-hour blocks 00–22 as columns, single-hue lilac-to-plum scale 0–20% with values in each cell, higher at night (00–06) and on Friday and Saturday evenings; hatched grey cells for slots with fewer than 5 calls, a legend stating that cut-off, subtitle 'illustrative mock-up, values invented', clean data-visualization style. + style block

lessons.title: Histogram
lessons.alt: Histogram example on made-up Team Nova data. A histogram of seconds to pick up for 2,700 answered rings, January 2026.

blocks.p: You want to see how values are spread, not just the average.
Bins should be equal width; mark any grouped bin.

blocks.code: A histogram of seconds to pick up for 2,700 answered rings, January 2026: 0–1 s 500, 1–2 s 760, 2–3 s 600, 3–4 s 374, 4–5 s 250 in plum; 5–6 s 110, 6–7 s 56, 7–10 s 30, 10+ s 20 in amber; the two last bins outlined as grouped (wider) bins; a dashed vertical line at 5 s labeled '216 late (8.0% of 2,700 answered)', median 2–3 s noted, clean modern data-visualization style. + style block

lessons.title: Scatter Plot
lessons.alt: Scatter Plot example on made-up Team Nova data. A scatter plot of 12 interpreters, x = occupancy 55–90%, y = late-answer rate 0–14%, bubble size = rings.

blocks.p: You check whether two measures move together, item by item.
A pattern is not proof of cause.

blocks.code: A scatter plot of 12 interpreters, x = occupancy 55–90%, y = late-answer rate 0–14%, bubble size = rings: points rise from Int-01 (58%, 4.1%, 180 rings) to Int-10 (88%, 12.5%, 290 rings) along a dashed trend line; one outlier Int-11 (62%, 10.4%, 120 rings) in amber with the callout 'late but not busy, check training, not workload'; footnote 'a pattern is not proof of cause', clean data-visualization style. + style block

lessons.title: Funnel
lessons.alt: Funnel example on made-up Team Nova data. A funnel chart of January 2026 calls, each stage part of the one before.

blocks.p: Each stage is a real step and you want to see where volume drops.
Only real steps where each stage is part of the one before.

blocks.code: A funnel chart of January 2026 calls, each stage part of the one before: Offered 3,000 (100%) → Rang an interpreter 2,820 (94.0%) → Picked up 2,700 (90.0%) → Picked up within 5 s 2,484 (82.8%); widths proportional, plum to amber gradient, drop labels on the right '− 180 abandoned', '− 120 missed', '− 216 late', clean modern flat design. + style block

lessons.title: Chart finder: all 33 charts on one page
lessons.alt: All 33 example charts from the guide on one sheet, made-up Team Nova data.

blocks.p: The guide has 33 charts in all. You've learned the 12 most useful ones. Here is every chart, grouped by the question it answers, so you can find the right one when you need it. Charts marked ★ have a full lesson.

blocks.h: How is it built, and what feeds it?
blocks.p: Blueprint: You need to explain how a system or path is wired, like a technical drawing. · Diagram: You want to show which parts feed into one result, and how much each part brings. · Exploded Donut: You want to pull one total apart so every piece and its size is visible (a donut with its slices pulled out).

blocks.h: What is it made of, and what are the steps?
blocks.p: Layers: You want to show what a total is made of, as stacked tiers. · ★ Flowchart: You need to show a decision process step by step, with yes/no branches. · Roadmap: You want to tell a journey with milestones, like a project or recovery path.

blocks.h: When did things happen, and what should we pick?
blocks.p: Timeline: You need to show key events in order across weeks or months. · Cycle Diagram: You want to show a repeating process, like a monthly review loop. · ★ Decision Matrix: You must pick between options measured on the same criteria.

blocks.h: What is the headline, and what is behind it?
blocks.p: Infographic: You need a one-glance summary of the most important numbers. · Tree: You want to break one total into groups and sub-groups. · Iceberg: The headline number hides bigger causes underneath.

blocks.h: How do we brainstorm or take notes?
blocks.p: Canvas: You are brainstorming fixes around one goal, as a whiteboard. · Sketch Notes: You want a friendly one-page tip sheet people will remember. · Handwritten: You want a personal, informal note style, like a lead's notebook.

blocks.h: Is it going up, down or holding?
blocks.p: ★ Line / Area: You want the overall trend of one measure over time. · Run Chart: You want to check if a change is working, against a target and the usual level. · Slope Chart: You compare several measures between just two points in time.

blocks.h: Are we on target, and who is ahead?
blocks.p: ★ Bullet Chart: You show actual results against a target in a compact way. · ★ Ranked Bar: You want to rank people or items from highest to lowest. · Dumbbell: You compare a before and after value for each item.

blocks.h: What is the total made of, and how did it move?
blocks.p: ★ Stacked Bar: You compare groups and also show how each total splits into parts. · Treemap: You show many parts of one total, sized by area. · ★ Waterfall: You explain how a total moved from one value to another, step by step.

★ Pareto: You want to find the few causes behind most of a problem. · ★ Heatmap: You want to see when or where a problem clusters across two dimensions. · Small Multiples: You compare the same chart across several groups without clutter.

blocks.h: How are values spread, and are they linked?
blocks.p: ★ Histogram: You want to see how values are spread, not just the average. · Box Plot: You compare the spread of values between groups, including outliers. · ★ Scatter Plot: You check whether two measures move together, item by item.

blocks.h: How does volume flow, and who covers when?
blocks.p: ★ Funnel: Each stage is a real step and you want to see where volume drops. · Sankey: You show how one total splits into outcomes, and those outcomes split again. · Gantt: You show who works when, or tasks across time.

questions.q: Weekly offered calls for 29 Dec and 9 Feb are partial weeks. How should the line chart show them?
o: Leave them out without saying so
Double them to estimate a full week
Hollow dots, with a note not to read them as a trend
questions.e: Mark partial periods, never fill a gap with a silent estimate.

questions.q: Atlas 72 + Birch 45 + Cedar 27 = 144 of 180 abandoned calls. What share is that, and which chart shows it best?
questions.e: 144 ÷ 180 = 80%. A Pareto chart ranks causes and shows where the running total crosses 80%.

questions.q: A heatmap hatches cells with fewer than 5 calls. What is that cut-off?
o: A choice for this data, printed in the legend
questions.e: Thresholds are choices. Pick one that fits your volumes and print it in the legend.

questions.q: A histogram's last two bins are 7–10 s and 10+ s, wider than the others. What must the chart do?
o: Mark them as grouped bins so heights aren't compared directly
Make them the same colour as the rest
questions.e: Bins should be equal width. Mark any grouped bin.

questions.q: Busier interpreters answer late more often in the scatter plot. What can you say?
o: The two move together; this alone doesn't prove busyness causes late answers
questions.e: A pattern is not proof of cause. Int-11 is late but not busy, which points to something else.

sections.title: Final task
sections.summary: Answer one manager's question with two charts. About 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Final task
lessons.headline: Show it.
lessons.intro: Pick the charts, write the prompt, check the result, then reveal the model answer.
lessons.html:
Open the practice workbook. It has Team Nova's made-up data for January and February 2026. Use any AI tool (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) or Excel. Time: about 15 minutes. Pass mark: 4 of 5.

The brief: your manager asks, "Why did abandoned calls go up in February, and where should we act first?"

  1. Headline. From the Monthly KPIs tab, write January and February abandoned rate as "x% (a of b)".
  2. Chart 1. Which chart shows how abandoned calls moved from 180 to 199, client by client? Name it and check that the steps add up (tab Clients by month).
  3. Prompt 1. Write the 4-part prompt for chart 1 and paste the style block.
  4. Chart 2. Which chart compares February abandoned rate by shift (tab Shifts by month)? Write each rate with its n.
  5. Audit. Generate one of the charts, check it, and write a finding title for it.
lessons.keyHtml:
#Model answer
1January 6.0% (180 of 3,000); February 7.1% (199 of 2,800).
2A waterfall. Steps: Atlas −12, Birch +19, Cedar −9, Dune +9, Others +12 = +19 = 199 − 180 ✓.
3"A waterfall chart of abandoned calls from January 180 to February 199: start bar 180 in plum, steps Atlas −12, Birch +19, Cedar −9, Dune +9, Others +12 (increases amber, decreases lilac), end bar 199 in plum, value labels, y-axis from 150 with a break mark and a note" + style block.
4A ranked bar, highest first, from zero: Night 18.9% (68 of 360), Evening 10.6% (70 of 660), Day 3.4% (61 of 1,780).
5Any honest check: wrong or missing numbers, labels on the wrong bar, bars not to scale, extra colours. Title, for example: "Birch drove most of the rise from 180 to 199" or "Night loses almost 1 in 5 calls".
